episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: How much should neighbours know about each other?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Quesnel’s new Mayor vows to tackle public safety over the next 100 days ! and Entertainment 360 Acquires Brigade, a Management Firm Rich in Substackers, plus 13 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Who sets the frame for publicly funded murals in Williams Lake, and who is accountable for how a continuing mural series reads and is maintained? Topics include: Grant funding, sponsorship, and whether the $5,000 fees are truly paid commissions, Who sets the subject, selection criteria, and sequencing of a mural series, Comparison with the Mulberry Street Percent for Art model in New York, Public unveilings, reach of the artwork, and the role of artist statements, Long-term maintenance, upkeep responsibility, and accountability for the series.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Station House Gallery

articles.author: Khushi Arora, Local Journalism Initiative

discussion.central_question: Who sets the frame for publicly funded murals in Williams Lake, and who is accountable for how a continuing mural series reads and is maintained?
discussion.riley_position: Grant-funded murals are real paid commissions that give emerging artists strong public exposure, and the program is checkable even if imperfect; the real need is for transparent rules rather than dismissing the work.
riley_key_evidence: Two artists each received $5,000 from the public art grant jointly funded by the City of Williams Lake and the Downtown Williams Lake Business Improvement Association
Jorgensen's panel is the third in the Cariboo Reflections Mural Project, on the Cariboo Regional District building at 180 3rd Ave. N.
The Mulberry Street project in New York is a $184 million reconstruction including Jennifer Wen Ma's 'Wings of Everchange,' commissioned through the Percent for Art program
discussion.casey_position: The selection process, brief, funding breakdown, and maintenance responsibility are unpublished, so the series lacks an accountable named person and the town cannot yet confirm the artists had free creative choice.
casey_key_evidence: Patenaude's abstract mural is on the north wall of Sam's Restaurant at 179 Third Avenue North, and the restaurant owner still controls the surface
The reporting gives no selection criteria, brief, or breakdown of whether the $5,000 covers materials, scaffolding, or artist fees
Nothing in the reporting says who repaints or pays for upkeep in later years, and the series name 'Reflections' may function as an unwritten brief
discussion.resolution: They did not fully agree; Riley accepted the need to publish the series rules and ask sponsors about fee breakdowns and upkeep, while Casey held that the work is a real step forward but not yet settled until a named person answers for the series.

roundup.opening_frame: A day of local civic ritual and new councils at home, then a wide look at who makes, manages and polices stories, from newsrooms and platforms to galleries and creators.

stories.point: Williams Lake has honoured its war dead in public for decades: the cenotaph was built in 1968, moved beside city hall and rededicated in 1984, and a Korean War plaque was dedicated in 1994.
stories.bridge_to_next: clean pivot from Williams Lake's remembrance history to Quesnel's new council

stories.point: Quesnel's new mayor, Coralee Oakes, was sworn in with seven councillors on November 4 and vows to tackle public safety in her first 100 days.
Entertainment 360 is buying the talent firm Brigade, which puts Substack writers and podcast hosts under the same management umbrella as film stars like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore.
OrbitalWiki has a new feature that plays a note whenever one of the nearly 17,000 tracked satellites passes its highest point overhead, turning overflights into ambient music.

The nonprofit Mississippi Free Press spent years tracking county election details, including eighteen wrong polling locations in state voter resources, which prepared it to cover a US Senate race still too close to call.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both stories are about newsrooms doing local reporting with limited resources: from a nonprofit newsroom to journalism schools doing the same work.

stories.point: A new study finds that journalism school faculty are a hidden infrastructure for local news as students report for real audiences, and that burnout is a risk for those professors.
A new Royal Academy exhibition looks back at Peggy Guggenheim's Guggenheim Jeune gallery in London, which staged more than 20 shows and shook up a conservative British art scene.
B.C.'s Civil Resolution Tribunal overturned a $100,000 penalty against X, ruling that blocking Canadian access to an intimate image posted without consent was a reasonable step under provincial law.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both stories are about courts testing how far a government can make platforms answer for content.

stories.point: Meta, Google and TikTok have sued California's attorney general to block a law, AB 1709, that would bar autoplay and personalized feeds for users under 16.
Colombia's president blamed the ELN for threats against media outlets; Caracol Television evacuated its Bogota headquarters and no explosives were found.
The Swiss Renaissance artist Urs Graf, a mercenary himself, drew soldiers and prostitutes in pen drawings full of violence and melancholy that reflect Swiss martial culture.
The Tyee says reader support now covers roughly half its budget through more than 10,000 paying members, and it has more than doubled its journalism team over the past decade.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both stories are about who pays for and stands behind written work now that AI is changing publishing.

stories.point: After social media speculation that the novel Shy Girl was largely AI-generated, Hachette cancelled its US publication and dropped it in the UK, leaving authors scrambling to prove their manuscripts are their own.
Some local news outlets are giving up physical newsrooms, and a Northwestern Local News Initiative report looks at the cultural losses when staff no longer work under one roof.

New York has started a $184 million reconstruction of 70 Mulberry Street in Chinatown, burned in 2020, and plans to house the five community organizations that were there, including the Museum of Chinese in America, when it finishes in 2030.
Poe reviewed Dickens's Barnaby Rudge, was taken with its talking raven Grip, and the two writers met the following year.
stories.bridge_to_next: clean pivot from nineteenth-century writers to a documentary about an artist's life

stories.point: The documentary Romare Bearden: A Life in Collage, coming to DOC NYC, is built like a collage rather than a linear biography, with generous access to recordings of Bearden himself.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both stories are about artists, one dead and well documented, the other working today, and what shapes their work.

stories.point: A survey for Epidemic Sound found 64 percent of six-figure creators and artists feel large pressure to use AI, compared with 19 percent of the lowest earners.

roundup.handoff: Who gets to make work in public, under whose name and on whose wall: the roundup leaves listeners with creators working under outside pressure, and the Deep Dive picks that up with two new murals on downtown Williams Lake walls.

deep_dive.central_question: When a downtown Williams Lake wall becomes a mural, who gets to say what it shows: the painter given a blank wall, or a series that already has a name and a frame?
deep_dive.riley_holds: A mural is an open door: a first-time painter can put abstract work on a restaurant wall and a local artist can add a panel to a shared project, and both are a healthy way for a town to see itself.
deep_dive.casey_holds: A wall is not blank; a business or a public building hosts it and a series name frames it, so the town should ask who set the frame before it counts a new mural as a new voice.

beats.claim: The two new murals are different kinds of commission: one stands alone on a business wall, the other is a panel inside an existing series on a public body's building.
beats.evidence: Courtney Patenaude painted her first mural, an abstract design on the north wall of Sam's Restaurant at 179 Third Avenue North; Tiffany Jorgensen painted the third panel of the ongoing Cariboo Reflections project on the back wall of the Cariboo Regional District building at 180 3rd Ave. N. (Williams Lake Tribune)
beats.pushback: Casey: the series already has a name, a count of panels and a location, so a new painter joins a frame someone else built, which differs from a free choice of subject.
beats.leads_to_next: If one commission is framed by a series and the other is not, the question is how much room each painter actually had.

beats.claim: A first mural on an abstract design shows a town handing a new painter a big visible wall without telling her what it must depict.
beats.evidence: The Tribune calls Patenaude's piece her first mural and describes it as an abstract design, painted on a restaurant wall at 179 Third Avenue North.
beats.pushback: Casey: abstract work on a restaurant wall sits on a business's property, so the host of the wall still has a say in what the street sees, even if the article reports no objections.
beats.leads_to_next: If the wall's host shapes what goes up, the next test is how the finished work is shown to the town.

beats.claim: The unveilings turned a finished mural into a public event on the wall itself, where neighbours could meet the painter and see the work together.
beats.evidence: Presentations were held at each mural location, Patenaude on Friday, Oct. 30 at 3:30 p.m. and Jorgensen on Nov. 2; the Tribune's group photo names Cariboo Regional District vice-chair Melynda Neufeld among those present. (Williams Lake Tribune)
beats.pushback: Casey: the photo shows who stood in the line-up, and a weekday afternoon event reaches whoever is on Third Avenue at that hour, not everyone the wall will face for years.
beats.leads_to_next: If the audience at the unveiling is narrow and the wall faces the town for years, the matter is who the wall answers to after the event.

beats.claim: The Cariboo Reflections series shows how a continuing project can keep a town's wall looking like one story across many painters.
beats.evidence: Jorgensen's mural is the third panel in the Cariboo Reflections Mural Project on the back of the building at 180 3rd Ave. N. (Williams Lake Tribune)
beats.pushback: Riley: a shared series is also what lets a newcomer like Jorgensen join something bigger than one wall and gives the town a body of work instead of scattered pieces.
beats.leads_to_next: If a series gives continuity and a standalone wall gives freedom, the town has to decide who answers for the whole picture.

set_aside: Entertainment 360 buying Brigade, the Romare Bearden documentary and the creator AI survey (they are film, screen or creator stories from the roundup, but the Deep Dive material is only the Williams Lake murals)
Mississippi Free Press, Nieman Lab, WIRED and the other media-industry stories from the roundup
Williams Lake Tribune remembrance history (a roundup story, not part of the mural argument)
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: The third beat, on the unveilings, brings it home to Williams Lake: two walls on Third Avenue North, one at Sam's Restaurant and one at the Cariboo Regional District building, show how the downtown shapes what residents look at every day.
deep_dive.landing: They end on a question held open, not resolved: when a mural sits on a public body's wall as one panel in an ongoing series, who answers for how the whole series reads, the individual painter, the building's owner, or whoever organizes the series?
